snapshot.title: UPSC History: Rowlatt Act & Jallianwala Bagh
snapshot.exam_hook: 🏔️ UPSC History Hook: 1919: Black Act/Massacre. Tagore: Knighthood return. Dyarchy: 1919. Ali Brothers: Khilafat. Dyer: Shooter. 13 April: Baisakhi.

quick_notes.title: Rowlatt Act (1919)
quick_notes.detail: "Black Act". Official name : Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act. Allowed detention without trial for 2 years. Slogan : "No Dalil, No Vakil, No Appeal". Gandhi called for a nationwide hartal (April 6).
quick_notes.explanation: The Rowlatt Act, officially called the Anarchical and Revolutionary Crimes Act of 1919, was a law passed by the British government in India. It became known as the "Black Act" because it gave the British the power to arrest and detain (hold in prison) any Indian for up to two years without a trial, meaning no court hearing, no lawyer, and no chance to appeal. This led to the popular protest slogan "No Dalil (argument), No Vakil (lawyer), No Appeal," which meant the accused had no right to defend themselves, no lawyer, and no way to challenge the detention. In response, Mahatma Gandhi called for a nationwide hartal, which is a complete shutdown of businesses, shops, and work, to be held on April 6, 1919, as a peaceful protest against the act.

quick_notes.title: Jallianwala Bagh Massacre (April 13, 1919)
quick_notes.detail: Amritsar. People gathered to protest the arrest of Saifuddin Kitchlew and Dr. Satyapal. General Dyer opened fire on the trapped crowd. Result : Hundreds killed. Rabindranath Tagore renounced his Knighthood.
quick_notes.explanation: On April 13, 1919, in Amritsar, a city in the Punjab region of British India, a large crowd of unarmed Indian men, women, and children gathered in a walled garden called Jallianwala Bagh. They were there to peacefully protest the arrest of two local leaders, Saifuddin Kitchlew and Dr. Satyapal, who had been taken by the British authorities for opposing repressive laws. Without any warning, a British military officer named General Reginald Dyer ordered his soldiers to open fire directly into the trapped crowd, which had no way to escape because the garden had only one narrow exit. The firing continued for about ten minutes, killing hundreds of people and wounding many more, though the exact number of dead is disputed. In response to this brutal massacre, the famous Indian poet and Nobel laureate Rabindranath Tagore renounced his Knighthood, which is a title of honor given by the British King, as a sign of his protest and disgust. This event became a major turning point in India's struggle for freedom, turning many previously moderate Indians against British rule.

quick_notes.title: Hunter Commission
quick_notes.detail: Commission of inquiry into the massacre. Dyer was censured but not punished (House of Lords praised him). This further enraged Indians.
quick_notes.explanation: The Hunter Commission was a committee set up by the British government to investigate the Jallianwala Bagh massacre, which happened in 1919 in Amritsar, when British troops fired on unarmed Indian civilians. The commission found that General Dyer, who ordered the firing, had acted wrongly and officially criticized him, but it did not recommend any punishment for him. Later, the House of Lords, which is the upper house of the British Parliament, praised General Dyer for his actions. This decision, where Dyer was criticized but not punished and even praised, made Indians even more angry and increased their demand for freedom from British rule.

quick_notes.title: Khilafat Movement (1919–1924)
quick_notes.detail: Led by Ali Brothers (Shaukat & Mohammad Ali). Issue : Protection of the Caliph (Khalifa) of Turkey after WWI. Gandhi saw this as a "golden opportunity" for Hindu-Muslim unity.
quick_notes.explanation: The Khilafat Movement (1919–1924) was a campaign by Indian Muslims to protect the Caliph, also called the Khalifa, who was the religious and political leader of Sunni Muslims worldwide. After World War I (WWI), the victorious British and Allied powers threatened to abolish the Caliphate based in Turkey, which angered Indian Muslims. The movement was led by the Ali Brothers, Shaukat Ali and Mohammad Ali. Mahatma Gandhi supported the Khilafat Movement because he saw it as a chance to unite Hindus and Muslims against British rule in India. He believed this Hindu-Muslim unity was essential for the success of the larger Indian independence struggle.

quick_notes.title: Watershed 1919
quick_notes.detail: Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms (Dyarchy introduced). Rowlatt Act. Jallianwala Bagh. Start of Gandhi's first great mass movement (Non-Cooperation).
quick_notes.explanation: The Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms of 1919 were a set of British laws that changed how India was governed, and they introduced a system called dyarchy, or double rule, meaning Indian ministers were put in charge of some departments like education and agriculture while the British kept control of police and finance. The same year, the British passed the Rowlatt Act, a law that allowed the government to arrest and imprison any Indian person without a trial for up to two years to stop protests. In response to peaceful protests against this act, British soldiers fired on a crowd gathered at Jallianwala Bagh, a garden in Amritsar, killing hundreds of unarmed men, women, and children. This massacre deeply angered the nation and pushed Mahatma Gandhi to begin his first large-scale mass movement, the Non-Cooperation Movement, in which he asked Indians to refuse to cooperate with British rule by boycotting British schools, courts, and products.

topic_title: UPSC History: Rowlatt Act & Jallianwala Bagh
lesson_intro: Today we study the 'Darkest Chapter'. The Rowlatt Act (1919), which allowed the British to imprison anyone without trial, led to a nationwide protest (Rowlatt Satyagraha). This culminated in the horrific Jallianwala Bagh Massacre on April 13, 1919. This event changed the course of history, turning Gandhi from a cooperator of the British to an unyielding opponent. For UPSC, focus on the 'Hunter Commission', the 'Khilafat Movement', and why 1919 is a watershed year.
